blindSummary:
This country presents extreme danger to trans visitors — and is the only country in its region combining an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveller abuse case. The 2018 penal code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, extending to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the police publicly announced arresting transgender women in a resort city after private-party photos circulated on social media; an international human-rights organisation documented arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travellers: in February 2024, a non-binary model and designer arriving at the capital's airport on a tourist visa was pulled aside while their friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. They warned publicly that people who identify as part of the trans community should not travel to countries in this region.
blindOutOfScope: Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; only trans-specific risk to visitors is assessed here.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying international legal-aid trust country profile documents this country's criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression.

Two rights organisations' joint report to the UN human-rights review (Aug 2025) on trans rights in this country: documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination - a penal-code provision and a dedicated surveillance unit monitoring and prosecuting non-conforming gender expression, prohibition of legal gender recognition and an explicit ban on gender-affirming healthcare; the country disregards prior review recommendations.

Rights-group country review: the 2018 penal code explicitly and implicitly criminalises trans expression and identity; a 2019 decree prohibits healthcare practitioners from providing any gender-affirming care to trans people; legal gender recognition severely limited; cybercrime laws used to punish queer and trans expression.

Legal-information platform overview (June 2026): this country criminalises all same-sex conduct (up to 3 years under the 2018 penal code) and restricts gender expression, with consequences extending to foreign nationals (deportation on top of prison) and digital activity; prosecution generally requires a spouse/relative complaint unless a 'public scandal' occurred - an exception that swallows the rule.

Online news outlet (Feb 2023): a genderqueer/non-binary model and activist alleges a transphobic ordeal at the capital's airport - taken to an isolated room, made to remove her shirt twice 'for examination', touched inappropriately, and told to return to her home country despite a valid 10-day tourist visa.

International human-rights organisation letter (July 2020) to this country's attorney general re: arrests and convictions under the 2018 penal code - four men arrested after photos from a private birthday party in a resort city circulated on a messaging app, convicted of 'immoral conduct', 'imitating the opposite sex' and cybercrime provisions; each sentenced to 3 years, a fine and street cleaning.

International human-rights organisation report (April 2018) on LGBT activism across this country's world region - includes this country's criminalisation and an annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across the region.

Law-journal article (2012) distinguishing homosexual acts from homosexual persons: in some countries guided by religious law, acts are criminalised (even capitally) while identity alone is not - scholarly context for this country's legal-religious framework.
